newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Oil chief troubled by Colombian production outlook.
newsitem.headline: Oil chief troubled by Colombian production outlook.

text.p: The head of Colombia's state-run oil company Ecopetrol warned Sunday that the outlook for oil production was "very worrying" because of a lack of exploration activity.
The recently-appointed Antonio Jose Urdinola said output could fall as low as 400,000 barrels per day within the next six years if no major new finds were made within the next six years.
Last week Mines and Energy Minister Rodrigo Villamizar said crude output should climb from the current daily average of 623,000 barrels to more than 800,000 barrels per day by the end of this year.
But Urdinola warned that it might be difficult for Colombia to maintain those levels.

"The outlook (in terms of oil supplies) is very worrying. We're not exploring and we must explore more if (Colombia) is to maintain a daily average of between 700,000 and 800,000 barrels," Urdinola said in an interview with the regional newspaper El Pas.

"Our excesses of crude will likely disappear within six years if we don't correct the situation. If we don't make another significant find, production will fall to between 400,000 and 500,000 barrels (per day)," he added.

Urdinola's gloomy predictions contrast sharply with buoyant forecasts both within the state-run oil sector and among private domestic and foreign operators who work in Colombia under association contracts with Ecopetrol.
British Petroleum Plc chiefs forecast the Cusiana- Cupiagua field it operates in Colombia's eastern plains will be producing 500,000 barrels per day by the end of this year.
They also believe the giant Piedemonte field, also in the Eastern plains region, will come on stream before the turn of the millenium.
Official government estimates suggest that less than 20 percent of Colombia's potential oil-bearing regions have so far been explored.

In the El Pas interview, Urdinola hinted that he may look at revising association contracts with operators working small fields in order to boost their profitability levels, particularly in those areas where little previous geological information exists.

But he made only passing reference to BP's call for sweeter contract terms on the Piedemonte field. The government's Council of State came up with a fresh interpretation of that contract earlier this year which effectively boosts the short-term profitability of the Piedemonte field. But Urdinola said the "ball was now in BP's court" to decide if it wanted to continue in the area or not.
BP sources said recently they were at an "advanced stage" of negotiations with Ecopetrol on working out a new formula for production in Piedemonte.
Urdinola added that he was eager to see an end to the debilitating wave of leftist rebel attacks on Colombia's oil infrastructure.

The National Liberation Army (ELN), the country's second largest rebel force, specializes in blowing up the country's main oil pipelines -- attacks which have cost more than $1.7 billion in damage and lost production in the last 10 years.
The worldwide head of BP's operations, John Browne, warned that the British multinational, Colombia's largest foreign investor, may curtail its activities in the face of the continuing rebel threat.

"My dream is to take oil out of the war...it's of advantage to all Colombians, regardless of whatever side they're on, for us to extract oil ... that's to say no more dynamiting pipelines and no more threats against oil companies and those companies that provide security for the fields," Urdinola said.
